read.sections.0.text.note: 'Ăn mừng' for celebrate (glossary); 'lễ ăn mừng' for celebration. Nowruz kept as Nowruz. 'Từ đông nam châu Âu đến Trung Á': check geography terms. Nowruz is celebrated by communities with different religions and ethnicities; keep neutral.
read.sections.0.text.source: A tradition is a practice that people share and repeat over time. It can be a meal, a song, a game, a skill or a celebration. Many traditions mark an important time of year. Nowruz is a spring new year. Millions of people celebrate it in many countries, from south-east Europe to Central Asia. People clean, share special meals and enjoy music and dance. The community meal in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it matters because people meet, teach and welcome each other.
read.sections.0.text.back: A tradition is an activity that people share and repeat over time. It can be a meal, a song, a game, a skill or a celebration. Many traditions mark an important moment in the year. Nowruz is a new year in spring. Millions of people in many countries celebrate this day, from south-east Europe to Central Asia. People clean up, eat special meals together, listen to music and dance. The community meal in the evidence section is also a tradition. The older person says the meal is important because people meet, teach each other and welcome each other.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Check 'năm mới vào mùa xuân' and that 'ăn mừng' is used naturally.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: A tradition is a thing people do again and again, for many years. It can be a meal, a song or a game. Many traditions mark a special time of year. Nowruz is a new year in spring. People in many lands celebrate it. They clean, share food and dance. The meal in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it helps people meet, teach and welcome others.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: A tradition is something people do again and again, over many years. It can be a meal, a song or a game. Many traditions mark a special moment in the year. Nowruz is a new year in spring. People in many places celebrate it. They clean up, eat together and dance. The meal in the evidence section is also a tradition. The older person says the meal helps people meet, teach each other and welcome other people.

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Sự truyền lại' for transmission per KEY_TERMS. 'Hàn Quốc' used for 'Korea' (the UNESCO listing the English refers to is the Republic of Korea; the contested-name rule: the English says only 'Korea'). Check if a more neutral choice is needed. Kimjang, couscous, lakalaka and Tonga kept as in the English. 'Diễn từ được hát lên' for 'sung speeches': check. 'Bắc Phi' for North Africa. | Review: 'Korea' in the English is the Republic of Korea (UNESCO); Vietnamese uses 'Hàn Quốc'. Place name to confirm. 'Trong phần bằng chứng' phrase and 'dạy lại' (teach it back vs teach it) worth a check.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many traditions help older people pass knowledge to younger people. This is called transmission. In Korea, families and neighbours make kimchi together in late autumn. This tradition is called kimjang. They share the kimchi between homes and swap ideas. In North Africa, people learn to make couscous by watching and copying others. They eat it together at big family and community events. In Tonga, large groups perform the lakalaka. It is a dance with sung speeches about history and values. In the evidence, a young helper learns to make the bread and wants to teach it next year.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many traditions help older people pass knowledge to young people. This is called transmission. In South Korea, families and neighbours make kimchi together at the end of autumn. This tradition is called kimjang. They share the kimchi among the houses and exchange tips with each other. In North Africa, people learn to make couscous by watching and following others. They eat this dish together on big family and community occasions. In Tonga, large groups perform lakalaka. It is a dance with sung speeches, about history and values. In the evidence section, a young helper learns to make bread and wants to teach it again next year.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: Couscous explained as 'món ăn làm từ những hạt nhỏ'. 'Hàn Quốc' as above. Check naturalness.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Traditions help older people teach younger people. This is called transmission. In Korea, people make kimchi from vegetables. They make it in a big group in autumn. Then they share it. In North Africa, people learn to cook couscous. It is a dish of tiny grains. They watch others and copy them. In Tonga, big groups sing and dance the lakalaka. The songs tell about the past. In the evidence, a young helper learns to make bread.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Traditions help older people teach young people. This is called transmission. In Korea, people make kimchi from vegetables. They make it in big groups in autumn. Then they share it with each other. In North Africa, people learn to cook couscous. It is a food made from small grains. They watch other people and then follow. In Tonga, large groups sing and dance lakalaka. The words tell about the past. In the evidence section, a young helper learns to make bread.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Traditions can change and still matter
read.sections.2.heading.back: Traditions can change and still matter

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Thích nghi' for adapt per KEY_TERMS; may sound biological, 'thích ứng' is an alternative. 'Không bị đóng băng trong quá khứ' is a metaphor ('not frozen in the past'); check it is clear for a 10-year-old. | Review: KEY_TERMS says 'thích nghi' for adapt, but 'thích nghi' is intransitive in Vietnamese ('thích nghi chúng' is unnatural). Rephrased with 'làm cho ... thích nghi'. A native speaker should decide whether 'điều chỉnh' is better for this transitive sense (then the glossary word changes). [Reviewer changed: Con người thích nghi chúng cho phù hợp với thời đại mới. → Con người làm cho chúng thích nghi với thời đại mới.]
read.sections.2.text.source: Traditions are not frozen in the past. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal adds vegetarian dishes and starts earlier, so more people can take part. The new neighbour says the earlier time means they can come for the first time. A change like this can help a tradition keep its purpose: to meet, teach and welcome. It helps when the group talks about what to keep and what to change. Not everyone in a community follows the same traditions or gives them the same meaning. No tradition is better than another.
read.sections.2.text.back: Traditions are not frozen in the past. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal adds vegetarian dishes and starts earlier, so that more people can take part. The new neighbour says the earlier time means they can come for the first time. A change like that can help the tradition keep its purpose: meeting, teaching each other and welcoming. It is useful when the whole group discusses together what to keep and what to change. Not everyone in a community follows the same traditions or understands them in the same meaning. No tradition is better than another.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: 'Món không có thịt' for vegetarian dishes; check. | Review: Same as standard text. [Reviewer changed: Con người thích nghi chúng cho hợp với thời đại mới. → Con người làm cho chúng thích nghi với thời đại mới.]
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Traditions do not stay the same forever. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal has food with no meat. It also starts earlier. Now a new neighbour can come. So the meal keeps its purpose. It still helps people meet and welcome others. The group can talk about what to keep. People in a group may not all do the same things. No tradition is better than another.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Traditions do not stay the same forever. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal has dishes without meat. It also starts earlier. Now a new neighbour can come. So the meal keeps its purpose. It still helps people meet and welcome other people. The whole group can discuss what to keep. People in the group may not all do things the same way. No tradition is better than another.

watch.summary.source: This video was made at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, D.C., in the United States. The festival invites people from many communities. They share their music, dance, crafts and food. In the video, people at the festival talk about why sharing culture matters. Sharing culture helps people learn about each other. It helps them see the world in new ways. It can help people stay strong in hard times and feel joy in good times. Each speaker gives their own view. No one person speaks for a whole culture. When you share with respect, you listen to the people who practise a tradition. You also give them credit.
watch.summary.back: This video was made at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, the capital of the United States. The festival invites people from many communities. They share their music, dances, crafts and food. In the video, people attending the festival say why sharing culture is important. Sharing culture helps people understand each other. It helps them see the world in new ways. It can help people stay steady in hard times and be happy in good times. Each speaker gives their own view. No one person speaks for a whole culture. When you share respectfully, you listen to the people who practise that tradition. You also acknowledge their work.
